summary:
Somalia criminalises same-sex sexual activity, but the sources give irreconcilable penalties. The Human Dignity Trust country profile records a maximum of life imprisonment under the penal code it dates to 1964, together with the death penalty under sharia in some regions. US State Department reporting for 2021 gives up to three years, and its 2022 report gives three months to three years for "carnal intercourse with a person of the same sex". The statutory text cited by Wikipedia is Article 409 of the Somali Penal Code, carrying three months to three years for intercourse and two months to two years for an "act of lust" other than intercourse; Article 410 permits an additional security measure, usually police surveillance, intended to prevent re-offending.

Enforcement by the federal authorities is undocumented. The 2022 US State Department report states that no official reports of enforcement were available, and that impunity generally remained the norm for violence against sexual minorities. Reporting covering government-controlled areas nevertheless states that LGBTQ people are regularly prosecuted, so the absence of reported cases should not be read as decriminalisation.

The lethal risk lies in territory outside federal administration. Under local interpretations of sharia in areas held by Al-Shabaab, and in Jubaland, homosexuality is punishable by death, with the sentence at a judge's discretion. ILGA records killings of people alleged to have engaged in same-sex conduct: two male teenagers aged 15 and 18 together with a man aged 20 in 2017, a young man in 2018, and two men executed by Al-Shabaab in 2024. The 2010 US State Department human rights report had already documented the death penalty under Islamic law in areas under insurgent control. Al-Shabaab's leadership has publicly stated an intent to enforce harsh punishments, and senior figures claimed a "death chamber" for gay and lesbian people if they returned.

Non-refoulement is well supported. Benjamin Christman's February 2016 report on the treatment of gay persons in Somalia concluded that gay persons should not be returned to the country because of persecution risk, providing a basis for refugee status and for LGBT asylum claims. Reporting from 2013 records Somali refugees in Kenya facing death threats and racist discrimination while UN officials nonetheless pushed for return, and documents persecution as a driver of displacement. Human rights and LGBTQ activists, and people accused of homosexuality, have fled the country for fear of execution or assassination.

There is no statutory protection against discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity, as the US State Department reported in 2022. The Marriage Law of 1974 defines marriage as a contract between a man and a woman having equal rights and duties with the object of creating a family, which excludes same-sex unions from legal recognition.

Social stigma compounds the legal exposure. Sexual orientation is a taboo subject with no public discussion in any region of the country, according to US State Department reporting for 2010 and 2022, and severe societal stigma prevents LGBTQI+ individuals from disclosing sexual orientation or gender identity publicly. The population is around 99 percent Muslim and has lived through decades of civil war and unstable government.
tangentialFactors:
The penalty range reported for the same conduct varies by a factor of more than twenty between sources, from three months under the 2022 US State Department account to life imprisonment in the Human Dignity Trust profile. A visitor cannot know in advance which figure a given court would apply.

Two enforcement accounts point in opposite directions: no official reports of enforcement alongside routine prosecution of LGBTQ people in government-controlled areas. Neither resolves whether charges are brought under Article 409 in practice.

The boundary between federal administration and insurgent-held territory determines whether the applicable penalty is a prison term or death, and control of that territory is fluid, so the governing regime at a given place and date is not fixed.

Somalia's pattern of criminalisation, non-state execution and non-refoulement recognition resembles that of other jurisdictions where a functioning asylum case rests on documented persecution rather than on statute alone.
localsOnly:
Organised community presence is minimal. One group for LGBTQ people reportedly existed as of 2004; by 2022 the organisations that remained were few, very discreet and mostly online-based, holding events infrequently.

Sexuality and health services are constrained by the same social mores that produce stigma. Family planning services and fact-based information on human sexuality are hard to access, and Islamic social norms make public discussion of HIV transmission difficult. Since 1999 much AIDS/HIV education and care has come from international organisations, including the United Nations. Adult HIV prevalence was estimated at 0.5 percent in 2007, one of the lowest rates on the continent.

Article 410's additional security measure, usually police surveillance, applies to those convicted and is aimed at preventing re-offending, which extends monitoring beyond the sentence itself.

Disclosure carries direct professional and personal consequences: severe stigma prevents LGBTQI+ people from making their sexual orientation or gender identity known publicly, and people accused of homosexuality have left the country rather than face execution or assassination.
outOfScopeNotes:
The identity of the governing statute is unresolved. One source dates the penal code to 1964 and another to 1973, and the two do not agree on the maximum penalty: life imprisonment against three months to three years. The inventory does not settle which text is currently in force or which figure a Somali court would apply.

Whether federal authorities have ever charged anyone under Article 409 is not sourced. The 2022 report's "no official reports of enforcement" may reflect absent reporting rather than absent prosecutions, and no case-level evidence is available here.

No source in the inventory addresses trans-specific questions: legal gender recognition, amendment of sex markers on identity or travel documents, access to gender-affirming care, or rules on gendered facilities. Any statement about these would be unsourced.

Entry, visa and border-screening requirements for Somalia are not covered by these sources, nor is the treatment of a trans visitor at ports of entry.

Named territorial control is dated to individual reports and may no longer describe the ground: Jubaland and Al-Shabaab-held areas are as characterised in the sources cited, without a current control assessment.
